title: Clear muddy water with alum
summary: A pinch of alum makes the mud in cloudy water clump and sink, so chlorine, boiling or a filter can do their job. Find the dose with a six-jar test, scale it to a pail, settle, pour off and then disinfect: alum alone doesn't make water safe, and it does nothing for fuel or chemicals.

materials.item: Alum: canning or pickling alum, or plain aluminium sulphate with nothing else on the label
materials.qty: about 10 g for the stock, more for big batches

materials.item: Six clear 1 L bottles or jars, and six stirring sticks
Two clean pails or tanks: one to settle in, one for the clear water
Clean cloth or coffee filters for straining
Plain unscented bleach for disinfecting after
Pool or spa test kit that reads free chlorine (DPD)

steps.text: Collect the muddy water upstream of anything you can see polluting it: see [Choosing the safest water source](#guides/reference_water_sources).
steps.warn: Alum can't fix water that fuel or chemicals have reached (CDC find water). Use another source.

steps.text: Check the alum's label: potassium aluminium sulphate (canning alum) or plain aluminium sulphate, with nothing else listed. Canning alum is potassium aluminium sulphate (McCormick alum) and is our first choice.
Make a 1% stock: 10 g of alum in 1 L of clean water, stirred until dissolved (IFRC jar test). Label it.

Keep the alum stock and its syringe well away from the bleach, and use a separate syringe for each. Alum solution is acidic (coagulants lower the water's pH, HC aluminum), and bleach mixed with acids gives off chlorine gas (EPA bleach label).
Fill six clear 1 L jars or bottles with the raw water. With a syringe, add 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 and 4 mL of stock, one dose per jar (IFRC jar test). Very muddy water: 2, 4, 6, 8 and 12 mL.
Stir each jar with its own stick for about 10 minutes, then leave them 30 minutes (IFRC jar test). Do it at the same temperature as the water you'll treat (HC aluminum).
Pick the jar that cleared, to under 5 NTU if you have a turbidity tube, with the least alum (IFRC jar test). None cleared: run it again with bigger doses.
Scale up: the winning jar's mL of stock per litre × the litres in your pail. Add it as the pail fills, then stir about 10 minutes (IFRC jar test).
Leave it undisturbed to settle. Give it longer than the jars, and longer still in cold water, where coagulation is slower (HC aluminum). Keep it from freezing.
Pour or ladle the clear water gently off the top into a clean container without stirring the bottom, and strain it through a clean cloth (CAWST factsheets, EPA water).

Disinfect it: boil it at a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (EPA water; 2 minutes above 2,000 m, HC boil guidance), or add plain unscented bleach (Health Canada: 2 drops, 0.2 mL, of 5.25% per litre, 30 minutes; 1 to 2 hours if the water is colder than 10 °C, HealthLinkBC disinfecting) and check at least 0.2 mg/L free chlorine after the wait (HC emergency water, WHO TN11).
steps.warn: Alum doesn't disinfect. Settled water still needs boiling, chlorine or a germ-rated filter (WHO TN5). Chlorine is ineffective against Cryptosporidium (WHO TN11).

steps.text: Wearing gloves, tip the sludge out well away from the water source and any well (our advice), and wash the pail after decanting (CAWST factsheets).

notes:
## What alum does, and what it doesn't
Muddy water is cloudy because of fine clay and silt particles that carry a negative charge and push each other apart, so they never settle. Alum's aluminium forms positively charged particles that grab them, and gentle stirring builds the clumps into flocs heavy enough to sink (CAWST factsheets, Sobsey 2002). Some bacteria and viruses ride on those particles, so they come down too (CAWST factsheets).

How much it removes depends on doing it right. Under good conditions, coagulation and settling with alum cut germs of every kind by more than 90 to more than 99%; done badly (poor dose, pH or mixing), by less than 90% (Sobsey 2002). Sobsey also calls household alum treatment hard to optimise without training and equipment, which is why the jar test matters (Sobsey 2002). That is a big help, not disinfection: WHO says settled water still needs a proven treatment before drinking (WHO TN5). Alum does nothing for dissolved chemicals (CAWST factsheets), and it can't fix water that fuel or toxic chemicals have reached (CDC find water).

Why bother, then? Chlorine can't reach germs hidden in silt, and WHO wants water under 5 NTU of turbidity before chlorinating (WHO TN11). Clearing it first is what makes the disinfecting step work.

## Which alum
| Kind | What it is | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Canning or pickling alum, spice aisle | Potassium aluminium sulphate (McCormick alum) | Sold for pickling and preserving food (McCormick alum). Our first choice. Potash alum is used for household water in many places (Sobsey 2002). It carries less aluminium per gram than aluminium sulphate, so the jar test may need doses above the Red Cross range (our reasoning from the formulas) |
| Garden aluminium sulphate | Sold for blueing hydrangeas and for acid-loving shrubs (Bonide plant care) | Made for soil, not drinking water, and no source here clears garden grade to drink. A last resort, only if the label lists aluminium sulphate and nothing else (our judgement); some garden products add iron (Bonide plant care) |
| Pool flocculant | Varies by brand | Read the label. No source here clears pool-grade alum for drinking water: a last resort, and only if the sole ingredient is an alum (our judgement). Synthetic polymer flocculants are hard to dose and some are hazardous chemicals (Sobsey 2002) |
| Water-works coagulant: aluminium sulphate, or polyaluminium chloride (PAC, also called liquid alum) | What treatment plants use (CAWST factsheets) | Made for drinking water. A liquid needs its strength known before you can make a 1% stock |

Keep alum dry and away from children (CAWST factsheets). McCormick gives its powdered alum a two-year shelf life in an airtight container, away from heat and damp (McCormick alum). CAWST puts coagulants at about a year in solid form and 6 months as a liquid (CAWST factsheets).

## The jar test
There's no fixed dose: it depends on the water, so you find it each time the source changes. CAWST suggests jar testing to get the best from a coagulant on each source (CAWST factsheets), and Health Canada calls it a helpful tool for optimising coagulation (HC aluminum). The method below is the Red Cross field jar test (IFRC jar test).

**Make a 1% stock.** 10 g of alum dissolved in 1 L of clean water. Then 1 mL of stock holds 10 mg of alum, and 1 mL in a 1 L jar is 10 mg/L. The stock keeps (IFRC jar test). Keep it, and its syringe, well apart from bleach: alum solution is acidic (coagulants lower the water's pH, HC aluminum), and bleach mixed with acids gives off chlorine gas (EPA bleach label). With no scale, any spoonful in any jar of water still works for the test, as long as you use the same stock for the bucket afterwards: the answer comes out in millilitres of stock per litre. You just won't know the dose in mg/L.

**Set up six jars.** Clear bottles or jars, 1 L of the raw water in each, a separate stick for each (IFRC jar test).

| Jar | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mL of 1% stock | 1.5 | 2 | 2.5 | 3 | 3.5 | 4 |
| Dose, mg/L | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 | 35 | 40 |

For very muddy water, use 2, 4, 6, 8 and 12 mL instead (20 to 120 mg/L) (IFRC jar test).

**Stir for about 10 minutes, then leave 30 minutes to settle** (IFRC jar test).

**Pick the winner:** the jar that gets the water below 5 NTU with the least alum. Too little and flocs don't form; too much and the water stays cloudy and carries extra aluminium (IFRC jar test). With no turbidity tube, pick by eye: the clearest jar at the lowest dose, held against something white or printed (our adaptation). If none clears, step the doses up and run it again; if they all clear, try lower doses, especially with a stock you couldn't weigh.

## Scaling up
mg/L × litres = mg of alum. At 20 mg/L, a 20 L pail needs 400 mg (0.4 g); a 20,000 L tank, 400 g (IFRC jar test). In stock terms it's simpler still: the best jar's millilitres per litre × the litres in the pail. Jar 2 (2 mL per litre) means 40 mL of stock for a 20 L pail.

The Red Cross adds the dose in parts as the tank fills, half when it is a third full and the rest at two-thirds, so it mixes through (IFRC jar test). For a pail, pour the measured stock in while filling, then stir.

## Cold water
Coagulation is slower in cold water, and the pH at which aluminium stays least dissolved shifts upward as water cools (HC aluminum). For aluminium sulphate, Health Canada gives the best coagulation pH as 6.5 to 7 in water below 10 °C and 6.0 to 6.5 above it (HC aluminum). In practice:
- Run the jar test with water at the same temperature as the water you'll treat, because Health Canada says to study cold (under 10 °C) and warm water separately (HC aluminum).
- Give it longer to settle than the jar test did. Settling takes anything from hours to days, depending on the water (CAWST factsheets).
- Keep it above freezing while it settles (our advice).

## pH and leftover aluminium
Coagulants use up the water's alkalinity and lower its pH (HC aluminum). Too little alum leaves more aluminium in the water and removes fewer germs; in acidic water, too much alum raises it too (HC aluminum). Health Canada's maximum acceptable concentration for total aluminium in drinking water is 2.9 mg/L, set as a running annual average in a distribution system (HC aluminum). Without a lab, the jar test's lowest working dose is your control. If you have pH strips, check the winning jar: chlorine works best below pH 8 (Health Canada chlorine TD), so a small drop helps the next step.

## Disinfect after
Pour off the clear water gently, without stirring up the bottom, into a clean container, then strain it through a clean cloth or coffee filter (CAWST factsheets, EPA water). Then:
- **Boil it** at a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (EPA water); Health Canada says at least 2 minutes above 2,000 m (HC boil guidance), or
- **Chlorinate it:** Health Canada's dose is 2 drops (0.2 mL) of 5.25% plain unscented bleach per litre, 30 minutes (HC emergency water); HealthLinkBC counts 2 drops as 0.1 mL and says to double the bleach and wait 1 to 2 hours in water colder than 10 °C (HealthLinkBC disinfecting); EPA doubles the bleach for water that is still cloudy, coloured or very cold (EPA water). Check at least 0.2 mg/L free chlorine after the wait (WHO TN11): see [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water). For a big batch, the Red Cross bucket test finds the chlorine dose on the settled water the same way the jar test finds the alum (IFRC jar test). Old bleach: [test its strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength).
- **Or filter it** with a filter rated for the germs you need gone: see [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters).

Chlorine is ineffective against Cryptosporidium (WHO TN11), so for surface water a cyst-rated filter or boiling is the safer finish.

## The sludge
The floc at the bottom holds what came out of the water, germs included (CAWST factsheets). Wear gloves and tip it out well away from the water source and any well (our advice), and wash the container after decanting (CAWST factsheets). At least two containers keep settled and fresh water apart (CAWST factsheets).

## No alum?
Plain settling works too, only slower and less completely: CAWST's three-pot method settles water for at least 2 days, pouring from pot to pot every 24 hours, and the storage itself lets some bacteria die off (CAWST factsheets). A [biosand filter](#guides/build_biosand_filter) is the longer-term answer for a muddy source.
